slides.title: Hyperbolic Groups
slides.notes: Open by framing the chapter question: negative curvature is being translated from smooth geometry into the language of graphs and words. Point to the source span, but stress that this lecture uses original models and checks to make the definitions inspectable without reopening the book.

slides.title: Curvature Becomes A Metric Test
slides.notes: Use this slide to change the students' measurement habit. We are not differentiating a metric tensor, and there is no sectional curvature formula on a Cayley graph. Instead, every claim must be read from distances, geodesic segments, and how triangles sit near their sides.

slides.title: Three Model Spaces
slides.notes: Treat the three panels as calibration instruments. A tree is the zero-thickness model because every triangle is a tripod. A grid is the standard obstruction because large rectangles create wide corridors. The disk picture previews hyperbolic geometry without requiring a model-specific formula.

slides.title: Delta-Thin Triangles
slides.notes: Build the definition slowly from one chosen side. For each point on that side, ask whether it is close to one of the other two sides. Hyperbolicity is the existence of one uniform delta that works for every geodesic triangle, not just for the triangle currently drawn.

slides.title: Tree Versus Grid Triangles
slides.notes: Read the notebook-generated figure as evidence, not decoration. The tree triangle collapses toward a central stem, while the grid triangle encloses a visibly broad Manhattan region. The important comparison is what persists as the finite drawing is enlarged: branching stays thin, grid corridors get wider.

slides.title: Four-Point Diagnostic
slides.notes: Explain that the four-point condition is a computational probe for finite windows. It is not replacing the complete infinite-space definition, but it gives a robust shadow of the same phenomenon. The recorded checks show tree delta zero and grid delta eight in the sampled window.

slides.title: Cayley Graph Hyperbolicity
slides.notes: Now move from spaces to groups. Once a finite generating set is chosen, group elements become vertices and generator multiplication becomes edges. The free group drawing should be read simultaneously as a graph of reduced words and as the geometric object whose triangles certify hyperbolicity.

slides.title: The Group Definition
slides.notes: Emphasize that the definition is stable under changing finite generators because Cayley graphs for finite generating sets are quasi-isometric. That is the reason hyperbolic group is a group property rather than a property of one accidental drawing or one preferred word metric.

slides.title: Quasi-Geodesics Stay Near Geodesics
slides.notes: Use the fellow-travelling picture to motivate why hyperbolic spaces are algorithmically rigid. A path that is efficient up to fixed multiplicative and additive error cannot wander through a broad flat region, because no such broad region exists. Thinness pulls efficient paths back toward geodesics.

slides.title: Word Problem Intuition
slides.notes: Present the word problem as a loop-shortening process. In a hyperbolic Cayley graph, a non-geodesic loop has bounded local evidence of inefficiency. With a suitable finite presentation, that evidence becomes a Dehn-style reduction rule: repeatedly replace a longer side of a relation by a shorter complement.

slides.title: Infinite-Order Elements
slides.notes: Connect algebraic repetition to geometry. Powers of an infinite-order element form a coarse axis in the Cayley graph: moving by the element translates points along that axis by a positive amount up to bounded error. In hyperbolic groups this produces two limiting directions at infinity.

slides.title: Narrow Centralizers
slides.notes: Use this as a structural payoff rather than a full proof. In a hyperbolic group, anything commuting with an infinite-order element must coarsely preserve its axis. That forces the centralizer into a narrow corridor and leads to the virtually cyclic behavior that distinguishes hyperbolic groups from groups with flats.

slides.title: Flat Products Break Thinness
slides.notes: Pause on the obstruction slide because it prevents overgeneralization. Products often contain grid-like regions, and grid-like regions support thick triangles. This is why the chapter treats free groups as the clean model while warning that direct products behave more like flat geometry than negative curvature.

slides.title: Boundary Preview
slides.notes: Preview the next chapter without making boundary theory do too much work yet. Rays that remain within bounded distance represent the same ideal endpoint. In a tree these endpoints form a Cantor-like collection of infinite reduced words, while a hyperbolic plane model suggests a continuous circle of directions.

slides.title: Applied Lab
slides.notes: Turn the diagnostics into a student experiment. Ask students to enlarge the grid window, predict that the sampled delta should increase, then enlarge the free-tree ball and predict that the delta stays zero. The point is to separate finite-window artifacts from uniform coarse-geometric behavior.

slides.title: Takeaways
slides.notes: Close by reconnecting the vocabulary: hyperbolic spaces are governed by thin geodesic triangles, hyperbolic groups inherit that condition through Cayley graphs, word algorithms exploit local shortening, and infinite-order elements point toward boundary dynamics. The next lecture can then study ends and boundaries as geometry at infinity.
